subject: chopperMotorbike
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: custom chopper motorbike.
Style: Overwatch.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for building an Overwatch-style chopper motorbike with bold shapes and glowing accents, thinking through how the builder API handles joint hierarchy since the vehicle still needs exactly one root joint even without being a creature.

I'm sketching the rig structure with a frame, steering joint, front/rear wheels, and swingarm, then designing the chopper's look: raked front fork, fat rear tire, ape-hanger bars, V-twin engine with exposed cylinders, teardrop tank with flame paint and a glowing orange emblem, plus glowing headlight and taillight details.

Now I'm working out real-world scale — bike length around 2.4m, wheel radii and positions along the z-axis — and figuring out how the platform thickness offsets everything so the tires sit properly on the floor without sinking in.

I'm defining the stage height and wheel sizes, then sizing a rounded rectangular base platform that fits the bike's footprint with a margin on each side, and setting up the extrusion axes for that outline shape.

For the top surface, I'm planning a textured plane sized to match the platform aspect ratio, applying an SVG texture with hazard stripes and ring markings to give it a deck-like appearance, then starting to define the root chassis joint position.

Now I'm working out the skeleton hierarchy: placing the swingarm pivot and rear wheel axle under it, then the steering head with a chopper-style rake angle determining the fork's direction down to the front axle.

Now I'm planning the ape-hanger handlebars rising from the steer top with a swept path and grips, plus the steer and front wheel joints. Then I'm laying out the hardtail frame geometry—backbone tube from steering head to seat post, down tube toward the engine mount.

For the engine, I'm placing a V-twin with the crankcase centered and the two cylinders tilted fore and aft by 30 degrees, each built from finned discs plus a head via a helper function that stacks thin cylinder layers along a direction vector. I'm also settling on an Overwatch-inspired orange and dark navy color palette for the final look.

Now I'm deciding on the bike's paint scheme: gunmetal metallic base with vibrant orange panels, white racing stripes, and a cyan glow for energy accents, plus a custom hex-and-lightning emblem instead of copying the actual Overwatch logo. I'm starting to lay out the part list, beginning with the stage base platform and deck decal.

For scene dressing I'm planning small glowing cyan strips along the edges, a couple of low background props like a toolbox or crate with a wrench to tell a story without stealing focus, and maybe a holographic emblem card on a short post behind the bike. I want to keep the bike as the tallest element, so props stay under about 1.1 units while the bike with handlebars reaches around 1.3, and I'm considering simple glowing bollards at the rear corners to frame the composition.

Now I'm working out the wheel geometry using tori shaped as tires, oriented so their axle runs along the correct axis, with the rear tire wider and fatter than the skinnier front chopper-style tire by adjusting radius and tube thickness.

For the tread pattern, I'm using a custom paint function keyed off the torus UV coordinates—mapping the position around the ring and around the tube cross-section so I can stripe blocks only along the outer tread band, not the sidewalls.

For the hub disc I'm thinking a lathe or cylinder shape with radial thin boxes as spokes, maybe 10 for the front wheel, while the rear wheel gets a solid mag-style disc with a darker thick cylinder core.

For texture, I'll add decal planes on both sides showing a hex-pattern SVG hub with a glowing cyan ring, using cutout alpha transparency over a dark inner drum so the cutouts reveal darkness rather than seeing through to the other side.

For the front wheel, I'm deciding between a wire-spoke design (rods from hub to rim) versus a decal approach, settling on ten chunky bold orange rod-style spokes for visual punch while keeping part count manageable.

Now I'm adding a brake disc with caliper on the front wheel, then moving to frame construction — planning the head tube position and angle aligned with the fork direction, and sketching the backbone curve from the head tube down to the seat area using a smooth sweep.

Working out the hardtail design: curving the backbone from head to a lower rear point, then splitting into twin seat stays that angle outward to reach the rear axle dropouts where the rear wheel hub sits.

Adding frame rails...

Now placing the engine crankcase as a gunmetal box with orange side covers and cylindrical case details on either side.

The orange covers get a glowing cyan ring as an "energy core" accent, and I'm angling the V-twin cylinders at roughly 70° apart with finned bodies and rocker covers lined in cyan glow. I'm also positioning an air filter disc on one side between the cylinder banks.

For materials, I'll use the clockwork kit's metal presets for chrome-like parts and the glow kit for emissive accents, keeping the paint style stylized and warm-toned rather than cel-shaded to match an Overwatch-inspired look.

Planning the exhaust system now: twin pipes on the right side sweeping down from each cylinder head, curving back along the frame with a heat gradient from steel to blued tones, ending in flared megaphone mufflers at the rear.

I need to check pipe clearance against the rear wheel's width so they pass outside it, then add a flared cone tip at the pipe ends and small band-clamp rings along their length for detail.

For placing the clamp rings, I'm working through how the `along` helper assigns orientation frames to each part so cylinders align with the pipe's tangent direction, and considering whether to explicitly bind them to the chassis bone rather than relying on nearest-joint defaults.

Since there's only one root joint and every other joint has an explicit parent, I decide to always pass an explicit bone to each part for safety rather than depending on automatic inference, and start sketching a small helper to build joints and parts. I'm laying out the joint hierarchy: chassis as root, then steer, wheelF, wheelR, and considering whether to add a kickstand, seat, or headlight joint.

I decide roles like hinge aren't really necessary for the wheel joints since this is a vehicle, and I'll skip most optional roles to keep things simple. For the kickstand, I settle on modeling it folded up under the left side rather than deployed, since having both wheels on the ground plus a stand looks visually odd, and I start thinking through how to define custom paint colors.

Writing shading functions...

Shaping the radius profile along the tank path...

Working out the decal placement on the tank, I need to figure out the clock-angle convention relative to the sweep direction so the flame texture lands on the correct side with the right orientation and facing.

That confirms mirror: s<0 for the flames. Now for the decal projection, I'm thinking the side panel can hold a circular emblem with flames behind it on a single texture, and the rear fender can use a swept arc over the wheel.

Working out the fender geometry...

Defining the box-section sweep for the fender arc with cross-section dimensions, then setting up the shorter front fender arc around its wheel with its own angle range.

For the fork, I'm placing two tubes at symmetric x-offsets representing lower sliders and upper stanchions, working out where the top of the fork attaches near the steer head.

I'm setting up a helper to offset points along direction vectors, then confirming the front wheel geometry: axle at [0,0.42,1.12] with radius 0.34 matching the ground clearance. Now I'm computing the trail by finding where the steering axis intersects the ground relative to the contact patch, and noticing the result comes out negative, which I need to double check.

Working through it, positive trail actually means the steering axis hits the ground ahead of the contact point, which is the normal chopper configuration, so a large 0.36 trail value is plausible for this design. Now I'm laying out the apehanger handlebars, planning riser positions from the triple clamp and sketching a catmull path for the bar shape starting near the center and sweeping outward.

Adjusting the bar path so it rises moderately to around 1.42 rather than overshooting rider height, then curves the grip back toward the rider with a defined thin tube radius. I'm also adding black grips with orange end caps, a small brake lever spike, and considering a pair of small hex mirrors on stalks as finishing details.

Now I'm placing the headlight between the fork tubes near the steer column, with a gunmetal cylindrical housing and a glowing cyan-white lens disc for the lamp face, plus chrome disc mirrors with a glass-like glow.

Checking clearance more carefully: as the fork tube slopes forward going down, it drifts toward the lamp's z-range by the lower edge, so I need to verify whether the tube actually pokes into the lamp sphere at that point.

I decide it's safer to shift the lamp higher and slightly adjust its radius so the fork tube clears it at all y-values, since the lamp's x-extent already overlaps the tubes' x-position and I want the lamp to sit cleanly in front rather than intersecting.

Now I'm shaping the solo seat with a sweep path curving down and back, using an elliptical cross-section that flattens toward the rear, and planning a dark brown leather color with orange piping along the sides using sector-based accent painting.

Adjusting the seat path and checking it clears the rear fender over the wheel, confirming the chopper-style low seat sits close to the back wheel. Now I'm adding a sissy bar with rods rising from the rear axle area up toward the back of the seat.

I'm nudging the sissy bars outward so they clear the fender edge near the wheel, then working out where to place a small tail lamp on the rear of the fender, trying a position lower and behind the wheel so it sits naturally on the curve.

Settling on an orange-red glow (#ff3d2e) for the tail light to echo that Tracer-pulse aesthetic, with a small hex cylinder shape pointing backward. I'm also considering whether to add a rear license plate or hero-tag decal, but thinking I might skip that detail for now.

Adding footpegs (forward control style near the engine guards plus passenger pegs toward the rear), a chrome gas cap with a glowing cyan indicator on the tank, and an energy cell / battery box on the left side under the seat with a tech-glow label.

I'm placing a toothed sprocket gear on the left rear hub for the chain drive, using a procedural gear geometry with 36 teeth sized to match the wheel radius.

Now I need to add a smaller engine sprocket and connect the two with a belt loop—computing tangent points between the two circles to generate a stadium-shaped path that wraps around both gears.

Building the belt as a flat closed loop with a rectangular cross-section, since it's planar in the YZ plane I'll orient the extrusion width along X and thickness smaller. Now I need to work out sprocket positions and radii to size the belt loop correctly between the rear axle and engine sprocket.

I'm also checking for clearance issues: the engine sprocket at x=.17 with radius .067 may overlap with the frame rails positioned at x=.12 with radius .03, so I need to double check those bounds don't intersect.

Since the sprocket plane and belt alignment don't line up, I'm reconsidering putting both sprockets at a shared x=.20 and connecting the engine to this plane with a shaft cylinder, while shifting the rails slightly so the shaft can pass through without visually conflicting.

Now I'm checking the rear wheel and stay geometry: the left stay at x≈.17-.18 sits close to the belt path and the tire's half-width, so I'm nudging both stays to x=±.18 to keep clearance from the tire while still tracking close enough to the belt line to look structurally plausible.

I'm pushing the rear sprocket, belt, and engine sprocket shaft out to x=.22 for cleaner alignment, placing the rear brake disc and caliper at x=-.19 on the opposite side, and skipping the fender strut for now.

For part count, I'm planning to add detail generously — cylinder cooling fins (~14 total), ten front spokes, merged bolts and rivets along the fender, tire tread paint, engine heads, pipe bands, and hex studs — then sketching out a texture list starting with a flame-and-emblem tank side decal.

I'm listing out the remaining textures: glowing headlight lens, deck platform top, rear wheel mag disc, front hub emblem, plate text, a glowing battery indicator meter, air cleaner emblem, a holographic prop card, hazard stripe strips for bollards and ramps, a small handlebar/tank speedometer gauge, and a primary cover engine emblem. I'm also sketching an original hero-style emblem — an orange-ringed circle with a stylized hex and lightning bolt — and starting to plan hazard bollard props with glowing orange tops wrapped in diagonal stripe texture.

Now I'm working out the placement and sizing of a holographic emblem sign on a pillar behind the bike, checking it clears the bike's footprint without exceeding its height, and trying to settle on a base platform width and length that gives enough room for all the props relative to the bike's own dimensions.

Mapping out the chamfered-corner outline for the base platform...

Thinking about splitting the base into two layers within the 0.08 total height: a lower dark layer from 0 to 0.05, then a smaller inset deck plate from 0.05 to 0.08 with decal texture and glowing edge strips.

Now I'm working out the glowing cyan edge strip around the lower layer's perimeter — a closed polyline sweep following the inset outline, offset slightly outward, with a small box cross-section for the emissive trim. Adding rounded caps where the closed polyline meets...

Then I'm moving to the deck texture plane, sizing it to the inset top deck outline and figuring out the correct facing direction and texture orientation so it sits flush and upright on the board.

Working through the cross product, right ends up pointing toward +X, so the drawing's width maps to world X and its length maps to world Z — meaning I need a portrait-oriented plane, roughly 1.0 by 3.2. I'll design the deck pattern with hazard stripes along the long edges, lane lines, a small center emblem, and chevrons near the front end, keeping details toward the ends since the bike covers the middle.

I'm deciding to avoid putting readable text directly on the deck since orientation is tricky, and instead reserve text for the rear plate, which faces −Z and should read upright to a viewer standing behind the vehicle given the default up-axis.

Now I'm figuring out where to put the gauge pod -- considering tank-top placement near the handlebar area, tilting it slightly up and back so it's visible to the rider, and working out its exact position and facing direction relative to the tank's surface.

Adjusting the tank's backbone path and radius profile so it tapers smoothly from a rounded top to a narrower base, making sure the hidden backbone stays enclosed within the tank's silhouette.

I'm checking for overlap between the backbone curve and seat at the rear, finding the seat sits a bit too high for a chopper look, so I'm lowering the backbone points to bring the seat height down closer to .65.

Then I'm fitting the fuel tank onto the backbone by checking the vertical offsets at each z-position, adjusting the tank's y-path so its bottom edge roughly sits on the backbone curve with only a small acceptable gap near the tail.

Now I'm positioning the seat behind the tank, checking it clears the tank's rear edge and sits properly on the backbone — though the overlap between the seat's front and the tank's rear needs a closer look since the radii suggest they might intersect.

I'm now working on the front end: placing the head tube around the steering axis, setting the fork tube offsets, and computing the stanchion start and end points relative to the steering joint position.

Next I'm positioning the handlebar at the top clamp and checking the headlight placement against the fork's parametric path, verifying clearances by solving for the parameter u where the fork curve passes near the lamp height.

I'll set the lamp center around [0,1.06,0.62] with small overlap tolerated, and add chrome support rods connecting the fork tubes to the lamp sides. Now I'm setting up the Three.js imports and helper functions to begin writing the actual geometry code.

Setting up geometry constants for wheel radii, axle positions, and the fork vector pointing from the head toward the front axle.

Now I'm defining the color palette: orange body tones with highlight/shadow variants, navy accents, white, cyan, black, and rubber/steel colors, plus a helper function for creating hemisphere-style gradient paints.

Defining color paint helpers...

Writing tire paint logic...

I'll scale the tire torus along z to fatten it, confirming scale applies in local axle space after rotation. Then I'm sketching a reusable wheel-assembly function to build front and rear wheels separately, working out the rear tire's major/tube radii so the scaled sidewall still lands at the correct outer radius.

Now I'm checking the rear drum cylinder and side decal placement against the tire's inner hole radius, making sure the wheel disc sits properly inside the torus tube without poking through its cross-section at different radial positions.

Checking occlusion at larger radii confirms the decal gets partially hidden by the tire past about r=.17, so I'll place the disc faces closer in at x=±.125 with a .165 radius decal, and extend the hub caps outward to x=±.19 with a .06 radius cylinder for visibility.

Working out the front wheel rim torus, chrome spoke geometry, and hub/brake disc layout with chunky orange spokes bridging hub to rim.

For the spokes, I'm computing radial vectors in the YZ plane for each of 12 angles, placing rod endpoints from hub to rim with alternating x-offsets, using the rod helper with color passed right after radius. Then I'm setting up a gear geometry for the drive sprocket with teeth count, module, bore, and hole parameters.

Now I'm working out hub, rim, and hole dimensions for the sprocket based on bore, module, and pitch values, then deciding on a paint finish — leaning away from gold since it clashes with the orange/navy/white/cyan palette, and considering an anodized navy finish instead.

I'm shifting to the gear part placement with steel metal and alignment along the X axis, adding a chrome rear brake disc, then setting up the crankcase box dimensions and position, debating whether to keep it simple with flat primitives or add bevel detail via extrusion.

Now I'm planning the side covers: an orange primary cover with an emblem decal on one side, and an "energy core" styled cover with a glowing cyan disc and ring on the other. I'm also working out the cylinder geometry for the V-twin engine, calculating the base positions and angles so the cylinders emerge correctly from the top of the crankcase.

Checking the downtube path clears the engine cylinder at the point where y is .73, confirming the frame tube doesn't collide with the front cylinder's extent. Now I'm computing the normalized direction vector for the front cylinder.

Writing cylinder helper function...

I'm placing the air cleaner on the left side opposite the exhaust pipes, checking its disc radius and position so it doesn't collide with the primary cover or sit too close to the tank.

I'm adding a carb stub connecting the air cleaner to the heads, and designing a hexagonal chrome gas cap for the top of the tank.

Now I'm placing a flame emblem decal on the tank's side, sized to fit the tank's length and radius, and considering extra Overwatch-style details like hex-panel patterns or a glowing cyan energy tube along the frame rail.

I'm adding twin glowing rods beneath the crankcase on a navy skid plate for that hover-bike underglow look, then shifting focus to the front fork—deciding to go with a springer-style design using rigid legs plus coil springs instead of a telescopic fork.

I'm sketching out the exposed orange coil springs between the top clamp and slider, with a thin chrome stanchion inside, and working through the triangle budget to keep the spiral geometry lightweight across both springs.

Still defining fork geometry...

I'm setting up the clamps and head tube rod positions, then defining the steer bone joint hierarchy connecting chassis to the front wheel axle through the fork.

Now I'm working out the kickstand hinge joint position and deciding its rest pose should be tucked/folded rather than deployed, since this is a static rest state rather than weight-bearing.

I'm weighing whether to add extra detail parts like a brake caliper disc, a cell canister, or tool tube, but deciding most of these conflict with existing geometry or aren't worth the complexity, so I'm considering simpler additions like chrome tank straps looped around the tank using a surface loop function instead.

Writing sweep code for straps...

I'm also planning to add seat stitching and rivets, then move on to designing the headlight housing with a cyan hexagonal lens and a half-visor "eyebrow" shape for an Overwatch-style look.

For the brow visor, I'm sketching a simple outline shape and extruding it forward with slight thickness, positioning it above the lamp with rounded bevels. I'm also considering adding a single mirror pair for extra charm, with a stalk rod extending from the bar end to a mirror housing.

I'm adjusting the handlebar path and grip positions so the overall height stays reasonable, lowering the bar peak and keeping the mirror stalk modest in height. For the mirror itself, I'm planning a small cylinder shell oriented toward the rider with an orange rim and a glowing cyan glass face.

Now I'm designing the rear wheel's mag wheel texture: a dark rim background, a cyan ring outline, orange spokes radiating out, and a hex-shaped hub in the center, all drawn as a solid non-transparent circle texture rather than cutouts.

I'm also laying out the full texture set I need: tank decal, lens, deck grip, mag wheel, emblem cover, a glowing cyan hexcore, plate, hazard stripes, holo panel, air cleaner intake, and a gauge face -- about eleven textures total. Starting on the tank decal SVG now with flame tongue shapes in the design.

Still writing flame path...

Still writing path curves...

For the flames, I'm stacking three tongues of different lengths at varying heights with a navy outline pass, then layering orange/yellow fills and smaller white/cyan inner highlights to make them pop against the orange tank.

Now I'm placing a navy-and-orange emblem circle near the front-left of the tank with a hexagon and lightning bolt glyph inside, building it as a reusable function. Then I'm starting on the headlight lens texture with a glowing background circle.

Actually I'd rather generate hazard stripes procedurally with TS loops instead of SVG patterns — a helper function producing skewed orange parallelogram polygons on a dark background, reusable for both the deck and hazard textures.

For the deck design itself (portrait 100×320, rear at top), I'm planning a dark blue-gray background with an inset lighter panel, hazard strips along both edges, downward-pointing cyan chevrons near the front, a faint dashed center guideline for tire tracks, and some light hex-grid patterning near the rear — skipping text labels for simplicity. I'm mapping this texture onto a plane sized to match the deck slab, positioned just above its top surface.

Now I'm reconsidering the deck slab geometry: I'll make the upper layer a simple rectangular box so the plane fits exactly without chamfered corner overlap, while keeping the lower layer as the larger chamfered extrusion, with the plane sitting just above the box surface so it doesn't clip with the tires. I'm also working out a glow strip that traces the lower layer's perimeter, protruding slightly beyond the face at mid-height, generated from the same outline array used for the lower layer.

For that glow strip I'm settling on a simple hexagonal tube swept along the closed polyline with radius around .01, which naturally avoids caps or seams since the path is closed. Then I'm moving on to placing props, starting with two hazard bollards near the back edge, each with a cylinder body, glowing top cap, and base ring.

Thinking through the rear layout more, I want a holo emblem pillar at one rear corner angled toward the front, and I'm considering a crate/toolbox stack at the opposite rear corner, while deciding whether small bollards near the front corners would crowd the clear space I want to preserve there.

I'm defining the holo card geometry — setting its base position, size, and orientation so it reads as a symmetrical glowing emblem card mounted on a short pillar with a hex base.

Now I'm adding a toolbox with lid and handle, plus a wrench shape built as an extruded outline with a jaw and head approximated by a small polygon.

Defining wrench outline coordinates...

I'll skip adding separate text details, and for bolts/studs I'll use a helper function that merges small sphere geometries together via BufferGeometryUtils for efficiency.

Now I'm placing rivets along the rear fender's arc by computing positions manually in a loop from one angle to another, offsetting spheres outward along the fender's curved surface at a small radius for a chrome rivet look.

For the front fender, I'm defining an arc concentric to the front wheel attached to the steer bone, running from roughly 65° to -30°, and thinking through how fork rake affects the fender's orientation in world coordinates relative to the wheel axle.

I'm checking that the fender's half-width fits between the fork legs, then working out small connecting tabs: short rods running from points on the fender at φ=20° out to the fork legs to brace the fender in place.

Tracing the fork's line against the fender's height reveals the fork leg sits noticeably behind the fender top at the same y-value, since the fork rakes back at roughly 47° from vertical — the leg passes through the axle angling up and back, while the wheel top sits ahead of it. That's just the expected chopper-style geometry with a raked front end.

I'm adding support stays connecting the fork's lower slider to the fender, computing a few sample points to confirm the rod lengths look reasonable (~.24 units, chrome, thin radius). I'm keeping a thin front fender since it adds style and partially covers the spokes, then setting up the arc function parameters for sweeping the fender's cross-section and defining the rear fender's box profile radius.

Switching approach — instead of trusting the arc sweep's binormal orientation (risky since a wrong frame could make the fender flat in the wrong dimension), I'm considering extruding a flat arc-band polygon (outer/inner radius in the z-y plane) along the X axis to form the fender shape more reliably, since lathe only supports full revolutions and won't give a partial arch.

For the belt, extrude can't make a hollow shape, so I'll just sweep a thin round tube instead — simpler than a box section and avoids the rx/ry orientation confusion, using a small radius around .009.

I'll make it a black rubber cord, skipping explicit teeth detail. Now I'm computing the convex hull of the belt's 2D cross-section points using a monotone chain algorithm, sorting points and building upper/lower hull chains via cross products.

I'm deciding whether to connect these hull points with a closed centripetal Catmull-Rom curve or just use a plain closed polyline -- given the mix of long straight spans and dense arc points, a faceted polyline with roughly 24 points per circle should look clean enough without overshoot risk.

Now I'm working out the belt geometry: rear sprocket pitch/belt radii, engine sprocket pitch/belt radii, 20 sample points per circle, and checking that the belt path at x=.22 clears the seat stay (radius .025 at x=.18) and other frame parts.

I'm positioning the engine sprocket shaft and transmission housing, adjusting z-coordinates so the shaft and sprocket don't collide with the crankcase or rail, settling on center [0.22, .40, -.2] with pitch radius .067 and belt distance .75 to the rear sprocket. Now I'm defining the rear axle rod and planning the dropouts.

Still working out stay and rail geometry...

I'm trying to anchor both rails and the backbone near the head tube junction, computing specific points along the fork and head tube parametrization to find where they should begin.

Checking further back, the backbone stays mostly hidden under the tank and seat through each z-segment, though near the rear axle it risks passing through the wheel/tire region at x=0, so I should route it to end at the seat post instead, avoiding the tire hole area.

Fender brackets and strut rods connect the fender to the stays; the exhaust pipe route stays clear of the tire and drum radius. For footpegs, I need to check that peg placement at x≈-.21 doesn't collide with the pipe's path starting from the head near [-0.08, .70, .32].

I'm checking whether the peg rod on the right rail clears the nearby pipe geometry, comparing their radii and y/z positions to make sure they don't visually collide.

Since dropping the pipes gets messy, I decide instead to move the pegs forward to z≈.38 and mount them via an arm rod running from the rail down and outward to a point where a short horizontal rubber cylinder forms the actual footpeg.

I verify the peg-to-pipe clearances numerically, confirming the arm stays roughly .1 units clear of the frame tube at each key height. Now I'm ready to actually write the code, and I jot down a naming scheme for the joints -- chassis root, steer, wheelF, wheelR, kickstand -- making sure wheelR's sprocket bone rotates together with the wheel, then start reasoning about the wheel joint's axle orientation along the x-axis.

Setting up helper function and type imports...

Writing import statements...

Still writing geometry setup...

Writing SVG texture code...

Still writing flame paths...

Adding hexagon outlines and spokes to the lens texture...

Writing more texture code...

Still writing plate text styling...

Now I'm designing a hazard-stripe texture for the bollards and a holographic hex emblem texture with cyan outlines, making sure stroke widths stay thick enough to render clearly at the target raster resolution.

For the deck texture I'm sizing it around 1024px max dimension, and setting up a gauge texture labeled "kW" instead of the default PSI unit. Then I'm starting to build the chopper's joint hierarchy -- chassis, steering, front and rear wheel joints, and a kickstand hinge -- defining their parent relationships and spatial positions.

Writing joint hierarchy...

Now I'm figuring out helper functions for drawing cylindrical shapes, realizing I can just use the builder's rod primitive with a radius array for tapered flat-ended tubes, specifying sides for the circular cross-section detail instead of writing a custom cylinder helper.

I'm defining the base outline points as typed tuples and setting up the extrusion parameters for the gun base shape, attaching it to the chassis bone with bevel and thickness settings.

Now I'm working out the upper deck geometry positioning so it sits flush on top of the lower layer, then adding a decal plane with the deck texture aligned on the correct axis above it.

For the glow edge, I'm sweeping a thin cyan tube along the outer perimeter of the lower slab, protruding slightly to catch the bevel, then considering small hex-studded corner posts at the chamfered corners.

Now I'm placing bollards at the front deck corners using textured cylinders with hazard striping since sweeps don't support textures, with glowing orange caps on top, and starting to think about adding a holographic post nearby.

For the holo post, I'm planning a hex base, chrome pole, a cyan-glowing torus ring acting as a projector, and a holographic card floating above facing along the default flow direction.

Now placing a toolbox on the right side near the back, with an orange-lidded box made from a body and lid geometry positioned at specific coordinates.

I'm adding a curved handle using a catmull-rom path arching over the lid, chrome clasps on the front, and a small cover decal, then considering placing a wrench lying across the lid for extra detail.

Writing tire geometry...

Confirming the argument order gives radialSegments=10 around the tube and tubularSegments=32 around the ring, with v=0 at the outer equator where the tread sits. With 10 radial steps of 0.1 each, the tread region near v<0.17 covers j=0, matching the outer tread band.

Now I'm building the rear drum and hub assembly: a rod spanning from -0.13 to +0.13 along the axle for the drum body, paired circle faces at x=±0.131 textured as magnesium-colored wheel faces, then chrome hub rods at ±0.21 with small cyan glowing caps at the very ends to suggest hub bolts.

I'm sorting out clearance issues on the sprocket/hub side -- adding a spacer rod between the wheel face and the hub to avoid overlap gaps, placing the sprocket gear just outside the tire's half-width, and adding a chrome brake disc plus a small orange caliper box near the rear wheel. For the front wheel I'm setting the tire as a torus with slightly thinner tread and a smaller chrome rim torus inset within it.

Working out spoke geometry...

Now for the handlebars, attached to the steer bone, I'm sweeping a curved path on each side with a chrome rod, mirroring the shape for left and right by flipping the sign.

Still placing riser rods and clamp geometry...

Still placing lever and mirror geometry... Now I'm positioning a gauge pod above the bar center, using a chrome cylinder oriented toward the rider, careful to offset it slightly so it doesn't overlap the handlebar mesh.

For the headlight, I'm defining its position, then building a cylindrical housing with a front bezel ring and a lens circle slightly protruding past the bezel so it stays visible from the front.

Now I'm adding mounting brackets connecting the fork legs to the lamp housing sides, positioning short rods between the fork and lamp geometry.

I'm sketching a windscreen/visor shape as an extruded outline mounted above the lamp housing, then moving on to skip the oil tank detail and sketch tapered exhaust pipe geometry with a varying radius profile along its path.

Checking the exhaust pipe placement against the rear wheel and hub to make sure it clears the tire and brake disc, since the hub rod sticks out further than I'd accounted for.

Good, both pipes clear the hub and disc. I'm sketching pipe1's path from the exhaust manifold down to the muffler tip, with a radius list that flares a bit too heavily toward the end -- I should flatten that taper.

Checking the second pipe's route past the transmission case and belt, then verifying vertical clearance where pipe2 crosses above pipe1 near the rear -- top of pipe1 and bottom of pipe2 leave a small gap, so that's fine. Skipping the heat shield for now and moving to placing support bands along the pipe.

For clamps, I realize I need to use the path's tangent-facing frames rather than the sweep's normal-facing frames, so I'll pass the catmull path directly into the along-helper to get proper orientation.
